scope: Trading and Fleet Carrier reference knowledge used by the Mongrels Field Manual and Ask the Mongrels.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Judge a trade route by real turnaround time, not only profit per tonne. Pad size, supercruise distance, supply, demand, jump count and loading time can make a lower-margin route earn more per hour.
details: Profit per tonne is only one part of route quality.
A station thousands of light-seconds from arrival can add more time than several extra hyperspace jumps.
Limited supply can prevent a large freighter from filling its hold repeatedly, while low demand can reduce the value of large sell loads.
Round-trip routes can outperform one-way hauling when the return commodity meaningfully contributes to total profit.
commonMistakes: Sorting by profit per tonne and ignoring station distance.
Choosing a route whose supply cannot repeatedly fill the ship.
Ignoring landing-pad size when planning around a large ship.
entries.operations: For squad hauling, publish expected profit per tonne, approximate trip time, pad requirement, current supply/demand and data age so members can decide whether the route fits their ship.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Treat third-party market data as a recent report, not a reservation. Check the update age, supply and demand before committing a long trip or carrier move.
details: Tools such as INARA rely on commander-reported journal/market data, so the displayed market can change after the last upload.
Busy high-profit routes can be depleted quickly by other commanders.
The older the update, the less confidence you should place in exact price, supply and demand values.
For a large operation, verify the market in game shortly before moving a carrier or dispatching multiple haulers.
commonMistakes: Moving a Fleet Carrier hundreds of light-years for a price that was last updated many hours ago.
Checking only price while ignoring whether supply or demand has already collapsed.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Economy types predict what a market tends to produce and consume, but current supply/demand and faction/system states determine whether a route is actually good today.
details: Extraction, Refinery, Industrial, High Tech, Agriculture, Military, Tourism and other economies have characteristic commodity flows.
Many stations combine more than one economy, so simple one-economy assumptions can miss useful trades.
Population, states and player activity can change supply, demand and price behavior over time.
Use economy type to find candidate routes; use live market data to choose the route you actually fly.

sources.name: Elite Dangerous Wiki — Supply and Demand

entries.ruleOfThumb: For mined commodities, avoid arriving with a load larger than roughly 25% of the station's current demand if preserving the advertised top price matters. Low demand can sharply reduce the price offered to a large cargo hold.
details: INARA currently warns miners when cargo can exceed roughly one quarter of local demand.
The price penalty is evaluated from the cargo you arrive with relative to the market's demand; the exact effective price can therefore differ from a third-party quote.
A practical planning rule is to seek demand at least about four times the load when chasing the listed high price.
Because market behavior has been adjusted in past updates, treat 25% as an operational rule of thumb rather than a promise that every commodity follows an identical formula forever.
commonMistakes: Seeing a high sell price but ignoring the demand column.
Assuming the price shown by a third-party tool is guaranteed for a Cutter-sized load.

entries.topic: Landing Pad Size & Cargo Ship Choice
entries.ruleOfThumb: A route is only useful if your ship can dock. Large-pad freighters maximize volume; medium-pad haulers trade capacity for access to outposts and other restricted markets.
details: Third-party trade searches normally let you set a minimum landing-pad size.
Large ships cannot use medium-only outposts, so a route with spectacular margin may be inaccessible to the ship carrying the most cargo.
For squad operations, a mix of large and medium haulers can be useful when the source or destination has restricted pads.
commonMistakes: Planning a route around a large freighter and discovering the destination is medium-pad only.
Comparing ships only by cargo tonnes without considering where they can dock.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Light-seconds matter. A short-jump route with a distant station can be slower than a longer hyperspace route whose stations sit close to their arrival stars.
details: Supercruise time is often the hidden cost in trade-route comparisons.
Large station distances also increase interdiction exposure and make repeated squad hauling more tiring.
When two routes have similar margins, the route with shorter station approaches often wins on profit per hour.

entries.ruleOfThumb: When possible, make the return leg earn money too. A slightly weaker outbound commodity can produce a stronger total loop if the destination sells something profitable back to the origin.
details: Trade-route tools can compare one-way and round-trip opportunities.
The useful metric is total loop profit divided by total loop time, not whichever single leg has the biggest margin.
Return cargo also reduces the amount of time a large hauler spends moving empty.

entries.ruleOfThumb: A Fleet Carrier is a mobile squad logistics base: 5 billion credits to purchase, up to 500 ly per jump, and 25,000 tonnes of total carrier capacity before service allocations consume part of it.
details: Fleet Carriers are persistent capital ships rather than normally piloted vessels.
The standard purchase price is 5,000,000,000 credits.
The carrier's total capacity is 25,000 tonnes; installed optional services and stored commodities share that capacity budget.
Carriers can provide configurable services, markets and docking access, making them useful for mining, trade, exploration, colonization, combat and squad logistics.

entries.ruleOfThumb: A normal Fleet Carrier jump has up to 500 ly range, a roughly 15-minute preparation period, then about a 5-minute cooldown after arrival. Plan logistics around the timer instead of treating the carrier like a normal ship.
details: The owner plots carrier jumps through the Galaxy or System Map.
A scheduled jump begins a preparation countdown that gives docked commanders time to board or disembark before lockdown.
After the jump completes, the carrier enters a short cooldown before another jump can be scheduled/completed.
Permit-locked destinations can restrict carrier access, so a normal ship's route does not always imply the carrier can follow it.
commonMistakes: Announcing a departure time without accounting for carrier preparation/lockdown.
Assuming a carrier can enter every system a normal ship can reach.

sources.name: Elite Dangerous Wiki — Fleet Carriers Update

entries.ruleOfThumb: Never plan a long carrier deployment from jump range alone. Tritium use depends on distance and carrier mass, and the active fuel depot holds 1,000 tonnes, so expedition logistics need a fuel reserve and resupply plan.
details: Fleet Carrier jumps consume Tritium.
Fuel consumption rises with jump distance and carrier mass, so a heavily loaded carrier burns more than an empty one over the same route.
The carrier's Tritium Depot holds 1,000 tonnes; additional Tritium can be stored as normal cargo and transferred into the depot when needed.
A carrier can strand itself operationally if it reaches a remote region without enough Tritium to leave, so deep-space routes should include a return reserve.
commonMistakes: Planning only enough Tritium to reach the destination and forgetting the return trip.
Leaving reserve Tritium in carrier cargo without ensuring someone can transfer it into the active depot when needed.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Carrier services are not free in capacity. Every optional service reduces the 25,000-tonne pool available for commodities, so a logistics carrier should install only the services that support its mission.
details: The carrier's total capacity is shared between stored cargo and the capacity allocated to optional services and stock packages.

A trade/mining carrier may value maximum free commodity space, while an expedition carrier may deliberately sacrifice cargo capacity for repair, refuel, cartographics, Vista Genomics or other support services.
Suspending a service reduces operating cost but does not necessarily recover the physical capacity allocated to installing it; remove services deliberately if capacity is the objective.
commonMistakes: Installing every service because the carrier can support them and then discovering the useful cargo space is much smaller.
Designing an expedition carrier and a bulk-haul carrier as if they have the same service priorities.

sources.name: Elite Dangerous Wiki — Fleet Carriers Update

entries.ruleOfThumb: Keep a healthy carrier balance rather than budgeting to the exact weekly bill. The base carrier has ongoing upkeep, optional services add more, and an operational reserve prevents an absence from becoming a maintenance problem.
details: The carrier's core weekly upkeep begins at 5,000,000 credits before optional service costs.
Installed active services add their own weekly upkeep; suspending services can reduce operating expense.
Upkeep is paid from the carrier's own balance, so owners should transfer enough credits to cover extended periods away from the game.
INARA can display estimated weekly upkeep and how long the current reserve will cover it when carrier data is available.
commonMistakes: Leaving the carrier with only one or two weeks of reserve before a long break.
Keeping expensive services active when they are not needed for the carrier's current role.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Use carrier buy/sell orders as a logistics contract. Set the price and quantity deliberately, ensure the carrier has the required credits or stock, and announce whether the operation is loading or unloading.
details: Carrier owners can configure commodity buy and sell orders rather than relying on an NPC economy.
A buy order needs enough carrier funds reserved to pay commanders who sell into it.
A sell order needs the commodity physically present in carrier storage.
Squad operations work best when the owner publishes commodity, price, remaining quantity, carrier callsign/location and the target destination or purpose.
commonMistakes: Creating a buy order without enough market reserve to cover the requested quantity.
Advertising an unload without checking that the carrier still has stock.
Posting only the carrier name and omitting its permanent callsign, which makes similarly named carriers harder to distinguish.
entries.operations: For Mongrel coordination posts, include callsign, system/body, commodity, buy/sell price, quantity remaining, pad/access restrictions if relevant, and whether members should load or unload.

sources.name: Elite Dangerous Wiki — Fleet Carriers Update

entries.ruleOfThumb: Check carrier docking permissions before relying on it as a squad rendezvous. Access settings and notorious-pilot restrictions can turn a perfectly positioned carrier into an unusable destination for part of the wing.
details: Fleet Carrier owners can control who may dock, including broad public access or narrower friend/squadron access.
The owner can also choose whether notorious commanders are allowed to dock.
For public loading/unloading operations, access should be checked before the announcement goes out.
commonMistakes: Posting a carrier operation to the squad while the carrier is still restricted to a smaller access group.
Changing docking permissions during an operation without updating the announcement.

entries.ruleOfThumb: An expedition carrier is a moving support base, not just a 500-ly jumper. Plan Tritium, repair/refuel capability, data turn-in services, rendezvous timing and a return reserve before departure.
details: Exploration-focused carriers often trade some cargo capacity and upkeep for services that reduce the need to return to inhabited space.
Universal Cartographics and Vista Genomics can make the carrier a practical data turn-in point when those services are installed and active.
Repair, refuel and rearm services can keep expedition ships operational after heat, neutron, landing or synthesis mistakes.
Publish a jump schedule with enough notice for members to dock, and identify whether the carrier will wait at waypoints or continue on a fixed cadence.
entries.operations: Before departure, record starting Tritium, estimated route requirement, emergency reserve, active services and who is responsible for refueling the depot from stored cargo.
